paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie became Master Librarians.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books Jack and Annie answered four old riddles, so they became Master Librarians. Morgan gave them secret library cards with the letters M L.

paragraphs.mainIdea: They must save stories from old libraries.

background.note: In ancient China, books were often written on thin strips of bamboo tied together.

background.note: A Christian teacher who brought Christianity to Ireland in the 400s. Today he is Ireland's most famous saint, and St. Patrick's Day is on March 17.

paragraphs.context: 2) Monks in the monasteries made beautiful manuscripts
paragraphs.simple: Monks made beautiful handwritten books to show how great God is. Most of their books were about religion.

paragraphs.context: 3) The first recorded people of Ireland were
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Celts were the first Irish people.
paragraphs.simple: The first people of Ireland that we know about were the Celts. Before the Irish became Christians, they had the Celtic religion and Celtic myths.

background.note: Old peoples of Ireland, Scotland, Wales and parts of Europe. Say it /kelts/.

paragraphs.context: 4) The great sea serpent Sarph was a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sarph was linked to the Milky Way.
paragraphs.simple: The great sea serpent Sarph was a Celtic creature. People connected it with the Milky Way. Today we only have small pieces of many old Celtic stories.

background.note: The long band of light across the night sky. It is made of billions of stars.

paragraphs.context: 6) In the ninth century, Viking raiders attacked
paragraphs.simple: In the 800s, Viking raiders attacked villages by the sea in England, Scotland and Ireland. They stole treasure and took people away as slaves.

paragraphs.context: 7) The Vikings were the greatest shipbuilders of
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Vikings built the best ships.
paragraphs.simple: The Vikings built the best ships of their time. Their warships did not go deep in the water, so they could land on most beaches.

paragraphs.context: 8) The Vikings were “settling men” as well
paragraphs.simple: The Vikings were people who made homes as well as fighters. In the end they started to live in Europe and became traders, who exchanged things instead of stealing them. They were also very good at making things.

paragraphs.context: Imagine a time in Europe over a thousand years ago
paragraphs.mainIdea: Long ago, monks made very beautiful books by hand.
paragraphs.simple: More than a thousand years ago, there were no printed books. People wrote every book by hand on animal skin, and they made their own ink and paint. It was hard work, but monks in Europe, mostly in Ireland, made some of the most beautiful books in the world. They painted pictures and gold on the pages.

background.note: Old books written by hand, with bright colors, pictures and sometimes gold on the pages.

paragraphs.context: Now imagine a warship that can travel far across rough seas
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Vikings made wonderful ships by hand.
paragraphs.simple: The Vikings made warships by hand. These ships could go far across a wild sea, stay safe in bad storms, and land on rocky land by the sea. The author thinks they were the most beautiful sailing ships ever.

background.note: The north of Europe: Norway, Sweden and Denmark. The Vikings came from there.

paragraphs.context: I’ve seen illuminated manuscripts at the British Museum in London
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author saw these things in museums and wanted to write about them.
paragraphs.simple: The author saw old hand-made books in a museum in London and Viking ships in a museum in Norway. After that, she wanted to write about both. This book gave her the chance.

paragraphs.context: I hope you find them as “wonder-full” as I do.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author hopes you will love these things too.
paragraphs.simple: The author hopes you will think these things are wonderful, just like she does.
paragraphs.tone: Playful. "Wonder-full" is a joke: it means "wonderful" and also "full of wonder".

sentences.context: They have already brought back a scroll from an ancient Roman town and a bamboo book from ancient China.
sentences.simple: They already got two things: a scroll from a Roman town and a bamboo book from China.
sentences.main: They have brought back a scroll and a book.

parts.text: They have already brought back
parts.job: Who and what they did: "have brought back" = present perfect, done before now.
parts.meaning: They already got and took home

parts.text: a scroll from an ancient Roman town
parts.job: First thing they got, and where from.
parts.meaning: a roll of paper with writing from an old Roman town

parts.text: and a bamboo book from ancient China.
parts.meaning: and a book made of bamboo from old China.

sentences.grammar: "Have already + past participle" tells us something was done before now. Find the two things joined by "and".

sentences.context: Morgan le Fay had told him that it was a very dangerous time, with Vikings raiding the coasts.
sentences.simple: Morgan had said that it was a very dangerous time, because Vikings were attacking towns by the sea.
sentences.main: Morgan had told him it was dangerous.

parts.text: Morgan le Fay had told him
parts.job: Who said it. "Had told" = past perfect: she told him before this morning.
parts.meaning: Morgan said to him earlier

parts.text: that it was a very dangerous time,
parts.meaning: that it was a very dangerous time

parts.text: with Vikings raiding the coasts.
parts.job: Why it was dangerous. "With + noun + -ing" adds a reason.
parts.meaning: because Vikings were attacking places by the sea.

sentences.grammar: "With + someone + doing" is a short way to add a reason or a picture: "with Vikings raiding" = "because Vikings were raiding".

sentences.context: People had to work very hard just to feed and clothe themselves.
sentences.simple: People worked very hard only to get food and clothes.
sentences.main: People had to work very hard.

parts.text: People had to work very hard
parts.job: Main part: who and what. "Had to" = must, in the past.
parts.meaning: People needed to work very hard

parts.text: just to feed and clothe themselves.
parts.job: Why they worked. "Just" = only; "to + verb" = the purpose.
parts.meaning: only to get food and clothes for themselves.

sentences.grammar: "To + verb" after the main part often tells you why: "work hard to feed themselves". "Clothe" (verb) means give clothes to.

sentences.context: It must be your darkest hour, when there is no hope left. If you ask for help too soon, it will not come.
sentences.simple: It has to be your worst time, with no hope at all. If you ask for help too early, the help will not come.
sentences.main: It must be your darkest hour.

parts.text: It must be your darkest hour,
parts.meaning: It has to be your worst time,

parts.text: when there is no hope left.
parts.meaning: a time when you have no hope any more.

parts.text: If you ask for help too soon,
parts.meaning: If you ask for help too early,

parts.text: it will not come.
parts.meaning: the help will not come.

sentences.grammar: "If + present tense, ... will + verb" is the first conditional: a real rule for the future.

sentences.context: Scholars today praise the brave Irish monks who helped keep Western civilization alive.
sentences.simple: Today, people who study history say good things about the brave Irish monks. The monks helped to keep the learning of the West alive.
sentences.main: Scholars praise the Irish monks.

parts.text: Scholars today
parts.meaning: People who study history now

parts.text: praise
parts.meaning: say good things about

parts.text: the brave Irish monks
parts.meaning: the brave monks from Ireland

parts.text: who helped keep Western civilization alive.
parts.job: "Who" tells us more about the monks.
parts.meaning: who helped to keep the learning and art of Europe alive.

sentences.grammar: "Who + verb" after a person tells you more about that person. "Keep something alive" = not let it die.

sentences.context: Before printing was invented, all books had to be written and copied by hand.
sentences.simple: There was no printing yet, so people wrote and copied every book with their hands.
sentences.main: All books had to be written by hand.

parts.text: Before printing was invented,
parts.meaning: Before people made printing machines,

parts.text: all books had to be written and copied by hand.
parts.job: Main part, passive: "had to be written".
parts.meaning: someone had to write and copy every book by hand.

sentences.grammar: Passive voice ("be + past participle") is used when who did it is not important: "books had to be written" = people had to write books.

sentences.context: I had dropped the rope so I could climb down the steps. But you two grabbed it instead.
sentences.simple: I dropped the rope because I wanted to climb down the steps. But you two took it first.
sentences.main: I had dropped the rope, but you grabbed it.

parts.text: I had dropped the rope
parts.meaning: Earlier I dropped the rope

parts.text: so I could climb down the steps.
parts.meaning: because I wanted to climb down the steps.

parts.text: But you two grabbed it instead.
parts.job: What happened next. "Instead" = in place of him.
parts.meaning: But you two took hold of it, not me.

sentences.grammar: "So (that) + could" tells the purpose. "Instead" means the other thing happened, not the plan.

sentences.context: The prows of their ships are often carved in the shape of a serpent’s head,
sentences.simple: The fronts of their ships are often cut to look like a snake's head.
sentences.main: The prows are carved like a serpent's head.

parts.text: The prows of their ships
parts.meaning: The front parts of their ships

parts.text: are often carved
parts.meaning: are often cut by someone

parts.text: in the shape of a serpent’s head,
parts.meaning: to look like the head of a big snake.

sentences.grammar: "In the shape of" = looking like. "Are carved" is passive: someone carved them.

sentences.context: He wanted to leave the gloomy island with its threat of Viking invaders as soon as possible.
sentences.simple: He wanted to leave the dark, sad island, where Vikings might attack, very quickly.
sentences.main: He wanted to leave the island.

parts.text: He wanted to leave the gloomy island
parts.meaning: He wanted to go away from the dark, sad island

parts.text: with its threat of Viking invaders
parts.meaning: where there was danger that Vikings would come and attack

parts.text: as soon as possible.
parts.meaning: as quickly as he could.

sentences.grammar: "As soon as possible" = as quickly as you can. "With its..." adds a detail about the island.

sentences.context: They were gathered from our storytellers—the old women who sing the tales of long ago, when people believed in magic.
sentences.simple: The monks got the stories from the storytellers. These were old women who sang the old stories from the time when people thought magic was real.
sentences.main: They were gathered from storytellers.

parts.text: They were gathered from our storytellers
parts.job: Main part, passive: the stories were collected.
parts.meaning: We got the stories from our storytellers

parts.text: —the old women who sing the tales of long ago,
parts.job: The dash explains who the storytellers are.
parts.meaning: the old women who sing the old stories

parts.text: when people believed in magic.
parts.meaning: from the time when people thought magic was real.

sentences.grammar: A dash (—) often explains the words just before it. "When" here means "from a time when".

sentences.context: It is such sights as this that inspire our bookmaking,
sentences.simple: Beautiful things like this sunrise give us ideas for making our books.
sentences.main: Sights like this inspire our books.

parts.text: It is such sights as this
parts.job: The important part, put first with "It is ... that".
parts.meaning: Beautiful things like this

parts.text: that inspire our bookmaking,
parts.meaning: give us the wish and ideas to make our books.

sentences.grammar: "It is X that ..." makes X important. "Such sights as this" = sights like this one.

sentences.context: As the ships came into view, their bright sails were filled with wind and their serpent prows blazed in the new sunlight.
sentences.simple: When the ships came close enough to see, the wind filled their bright sails, and the snake heads at the front shone in the morning sun.
sentences.main: The sails filled and the prows blazed.

parts.text: As the ships came into view,
parts.job: When: "as" = while, at the same time.
parts.meaning: When Jack could begin to see the ships,

parts.text: their bright sails were filled with wind
parts.meaning: the wind filled their bright sails

parts.text: and their serpent prows blazed in the new sunlight.
parts.meaning: and the snake heads at the front shone brightly in the morning sun.

sentences.grammar: One time part ("As...") and two main parts joined by "and". "Blazed" makes the ships sound like fire: scary.

sentences.context: It is better that the world should have some of it than none at all.
sentences.simple: It is better for the world to have part of the book than nothing.
sentences.main: It is better to have some of it.

parts.text: It is better
parts.meaning: It is a better thing

parts.text: that the world should have some of it
parts.meaning: for the world to have a part of the book

parts.text: than none at all.
parts.meaning: than to have nothing.

sentences.grammar: "Better ... than ..." compares two things. "None at all" = nothing, not even a little.

sentences.context: They seemed deserted as they bobbed in the shallow waves.
sentences.simple: The ships looked empty as they moved up and down in the low water.
sentences.main: They seemed deserted.

parts.text: They seemed deserted
parts.meaning: The ships looked empty

parts.text: as they bobbed in the shallow waves.
parts.meaning: while they moved up and down in the water that was not deep.

sentences.grammar: "Seem + adjective" = look or feel like. "As" here means "while".

sentences.context: It held her weight as she began inching along it.
sentences.simple: The rope was strong enough to hold her, and she moved along it slowly.
sentences.main: It held her weight.

parts.text: It held her weight
parts.meaning: The rope did not break under her

parts.text: as she began inching along it.
parts.job: When: at the same time. "Inching" = moving slowly.
parts.meaning: while she started to move along it, a little at a time.

sentences.grammar: "Inch" can be a verb: move a very small way at a time.

sentences.context: When there was no wind, the crew would take down the sails and row with oars.
sentences.simple: If there was no wind, the sailors lowered the sails and moved the ship with oars.
sentences.main: The crew would row with oars.

parts.text: When there was no wind,
parts.meaning: At times with no wind,

parts.text: the crew would take down the sails
parts.job: Main part. "Would" = what they usually did in the past.
parts.meaning: the sailors usually lowered the sails

parts.text: and row with oars.
parts.meaning: and moved the boat with oars.

sentences.grammar: "Would + verb" can mean "used to": something people did again and again in the past.

sentences.context: He hadn’t thought of Vikings as real people before—people with families and little kids.
sentences.simple: Before this, Jack never thought that Vikings were real people with families and children.
sentences.main: He hadn't thought of Vikings as real people.

parts.text: He hadn’t thought of Vikings
parts.job: Main part, past perfect (before this moment).
parts.meaning: Before now he never thought of Vikings

parts.text: as real people before
parts.job: "Think of A as B" = see A like B.
parts.meaning: as real people

parts.text: —people with families and little kids.
parts.meaning: people who have families and little children.

sentences.grammar: "Think of A as B" = believe A is B. "Hadn't thought" = past perfect: up to that time.

sentences.context: The great serpent was pressing its long neck against the back of the ship, pushing it toward the shore.
sentences.simple: The big sea snake was pushing the back of the ship with its long neck, and moving it to the shore.
sentences.main: The serpent was pushing the ship.

parts.text: The great serpent
parts.meaning: The big sea snake

parts.text: was pressing its long neck against the back of the ship,
parts.meaning: was pushing its long neck on the back of the ship

parts.text: pushing it toward the shore.
parts.job: "-ing" part: the result at the same time.
parts.meaning: and so it moved the ship to the shore.

sentences.grammar: An -ing part after a comma often tells what happens at the same time or as a result.

sentences.context: In fact, once the Vikings settled down, they became more than just a warrior people.
sentences.simple: Really, when the Vikings started to live in one place, they were not only fighters any more.
sentences.main: The Vikings became more than warriors.

parts.text: In fact,
parts.meaning: Really,

parts.text: once the Vikings settled down,
parts.meaning: after the Vikings began to live in one place,

parts.text: they became more than just a warrior people.
parts.meaning: they were not only a people of fighters.

sentences.grammar: "Once" at the start of a part can mean "after" or "as soon as". "More than just" = not only.

sentences.context: Just as Jack and Annie were not able to rescue the complete story of Sarph, today we have only fragments of many old Celtic stories.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie could not save all of Sarph's story. In the same way, today we only have small pieces of many old Celtic stories.
sentences.main: Today we have only fragments.

parts.text: Just as Jack and Annie were not able to rescue the complete story of Sarph,
parts.job: "Just as" = in the same way as.
parts.meaning: In the same way that Jack and Annie could not save all of Sarph's story,

parts.text: today we have only fragments of many old Celtic stories.
parts.meaning: today we only have small pieces of many old Celtic stories.

sentences.grammar: "Just as A, B" means A and B are alike.

darkest hour.meaning: The worst and most hopeless time, when you think nothing can help you any more.
darkest hour.usageNote: A strong, a little old-fashioned phrase. In this series it is the time when the magic story can help.

have no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

watch out.meaning: Be careful! Look out for danger.
watch out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

watch it.usageNote: Informal. It can also sound a little rude, like "Be careful what you do!"

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm or brave.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in place of.meaning: Instead of; where something else was before.
in place of.example: And in place of his backpack was a leather bag.
in place of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold on.meaning: To keep holding something tightly so you do not fall or let it go. "Hold on to" + the thing.
hold on.example: Annie held on to the rope as she climbed slowly up the stairs.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pull out.meaning: To take something out of a bag, a pocket or a place.
pull out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in the world.meaning: Used after "how", "what", "where" to show you are very surprised.
in the world.example: How in the world did you get on this island?
in the world.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

stand for.meaning: To be a sign of something; to mean something.
stand for.example: I am afraid it stands for their fierce, cold-blooded ways.
stand for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

too bad.meaning: What a pity; that is bad luck (sometimes said when you do not really feel sorry).
too bad.example: “Too bad for them,” she said cheerfully.
too bad.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

change the subject.meaning: To start talking about something different, often to stop talking about the thing before.
change the subject.example: But the monk changed the subject.
change the subject.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

save the best for last.meaning: To keep the best thing until the end.
save the best for last.example: “I have saved the best for last,” he said.
save the best for last.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

best of all.meaning: Better than all the other things; the best thing was...
best of all.example: Best of all, some were writing and painting in books.
best of all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as well as.example: We record Christian stories as well as the old myths of Ireland.
as well as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

believe in.meaning: To think that something is real.
believe in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

break into a smile.example: His wrinkled face broke into a smile.
break into a smile.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

break the silence.meaning: To be the first to speak or make a sound when everyone is quiet.
break the silence.example: Finally, Brother Patrick broke the silence.
break the silence.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in an instant.meaning: Very quickly; in a very short time.
in an instant.example: Everything can change in an instant.
in an instant.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

come into view.example: As the ships came into view
come into view.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

let go of.example: Jack reached the rocky ledge and let go of the rope.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make haste.example: “Make haste!” he said to the other monks.
make haste.usageNote: An old phrase. Today we say "Hurry!"

take good care of.meaning: To look after something well and keep it safe.
take good care of.example: “We’ll take good care of it,” said Jack.
take good care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

just in case.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

check out.meaning: (1) (informal) To look at something because it is interesting. (2) To borrow a book from a library ("check them out").
check out.example: Jack really wanted to check out the ships.
check out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

waste time.meaning: To use time badly, doing nothing useful.
waste time.example: But he was afraid of wasting time.
waste time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hand over hand.meaning: Moving one hand in front of the other again and again, like when you climb or pull a rope.
hand over hand.example: She kept going, hand over hand, along the rope
hand over hand.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that...
as if.example: The fog and the movement of the ship made Jack feel as if he was in a dream.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pick up.example: The wind picked up as Jack lifted his heavy oar over the side of the ship.
pick up.usageNote: "Pick up" has many meanings. Here it means the wind got stronger.

take down.meaning: (1) To bring something down from a high place. "Take down the sails" means lower them. (2) To lead someone down to a lower place ("take you down to the shore").
take down.example: the crew would take down the sails and row with oars
take down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pull off.example: Annie pulled off her scarf and put a helmet on her head.
pull off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

sand bar.meaning: A long, low hill of sand in the sea near the shore. The water above it is not deep.
sand bar.example: The ship swooshed onto a sand bar near the shore.
sand bar.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

all of a sudden.example: All of a sudden, Annie gasped.
all of a sudden.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

cause trouble.meaning: To make problems for other people.
cause trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

bits and pieces.meaning: Small parts of something, not the whole thing.
bits and pieces.example: we have only bits and pieces of many wonderful old stories
bits and pieces.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

settle down.meaning: To start living in one place and have a quiet life, after moving around.
settle down.example: once the Vikings settled down, they became more than just a warrior people
settle down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. Used to add something surprising.
in fact.example: In fact, once the Vikings settled down
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: (informal) To leave or run away quickly.
take off.example: Jack and Annie took off through the woods.
take off.usageNote: Very common. It also means a plane leaving the ground, or taking off your clothes.
